title: Fundamentals of Zen Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the two sides of meditation, stability and insight, drawing on a five-day session held with Seattle Soto Zen at a former Methodist camp. Nomon teaches "go back to one" breath counting as a place to stand in awareness, then loosens it toward open attention and the question "What is it?" A story of getting reactive with a student during the retreat shows how mental patterns become visible and lose some of their hold. Nomon then turns to limited and unlimited life, from Vizzini's "Inconceivable!" in The Princess Bride to Dogen's mist that leaves a robe damp.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Good evening.
Good to see you.
Hannah said something about getting full value from the talk, so I'll try to provide some value.
I don't know how to do it though, because we all have value, and everything we do has value, you know?
I think it's so easy for us to imagine in our minds that one part of something is the important part, and the other part is the warm up, and the other part is the after work, or something like that.
I just came back from a five day retreat, five day session, we call them Zen meditation retreat.
At one point I was giving one of the talks, and it occurred to me: I wonder if it's really the talk that's important, or the bowing before the talk, or the meditation.
Who knows what's really important?

I remember my teacher Norman Fischer saying to us one time, "Well, my real intention here, we give these long talks, and we've been sitting there all day, is to just take your mind off your knees for a while."
So we did spend a fair amount of time sitting there with our knees, or whatever parts of our body were feeling a little bit difficult.
It's such a powerful practice, the practice we call session.
And session means to touch the heart, or to touch the mind.
So it's not so much figuring anything out, or calming down, or getting better at something, but it's like: what if we really had some time to just touch in to what's here?
Can I make contact with myself in some way?
It's a great thing to do, and this is one that we do in collaboration with the Seattle group in our same lineage, Seattle Soto Zen.
They don't have a place of their own in Seattle, they sublet at an Aikido studio, but then they have several retreats a year, a few of which we do together.
This one is right in the middle of September.
They rent a church camp right across the water from downtown Seattle, a place on the Kitsap Peninsula, next to the little town of Indianola.
It's a Methodist camp from the 50s, which, like most church camps that were started in the 50s and 60s, there's not too many church groups anymore that use them.
The churches are shrinking, so they all become Buddhist retreat centers.
It's kind of inevitable.
It's the arc of the universe for church camps to become Buddhist retreat centers, and other kinds of retreats there too.
There was a little group from UW in one of the other buildings.
I'm not sure what they were doing.
But anyway, I just really recommend that practice, and I want to give you a little sketch of it if you haven't done that yet.
We get up kind of early because there's a sense of continuity.
Somebody runs around with a bell at five in the morning, and we were all out of bed.
We provide coffee.
I have done session where there's no coffee allowed.
It actually works okay, but I prefer the coffee kind.

The main thing about it, why it's even doable to get up at five in the morning and then pretty much be silent and meditating in one form or another all day, why that's possible, is because you do it together.
It's a real supportive community endeavor.
You really know the person next to you in the meditation hall, even though you're not talking, so you don't find out what job they have.
Maybe you can barely remember what their name is from when you briefly met them at the beginning.
But you get to be so close, because you know how they clear their throat.
You know how they walk.
You know how they arrange themselves.
Sometimes you love them, sometimes you don't.
I was thinking about our whole practice, and this retreat is an intensive form of it, but it's true of all our practice.
It's getting to know how the mind operates, which we take for granted, right?
We think, "Oh, I just think about stuff, and I do stuff, and I know what's going on."
But when we really stop and settle in, with the support of meditation, we see some dimensions of our mind, and we see some patterns much more clearly.
When we're doing Zen meditation, like all Buddhist meditation, there are two major areas, more or less.
Some schools of Buddhism divide these things up very clearly.
We tend to let them get all mixed together because we think, well, that's like reality: everything's mixed up.
But once in a while it's worth breaking these things apart before we let them merge back together, just so we can pick them up and see them a little more.
So, two aspects of meditation that we focused on for five days and you just focused on for an hour and change, which is amazing.
This is amazing, or what, right?
A group of people who could be doing lots of other interesting things tonight chose to spend their evening being quiet, being present and exploring something.
So, two aspects of this, one way of talking about it anyway.
One aspect is stability and the other aspect is insight.
For the Buddhist geeks, I'm thinking about the Buddhist terms, shamatha and vipassana.
And I can't read my notes.
Hold on.
A very small amount of optics will solve that.
When I first heard about this way of thinking, I thought, well, maybe there are some practices that are really good at the stability side and some practices that are really good at this insight side.
But more and more I think about it, every practice, every moment of our life, we have these two qualities that I'm calling stability and insight.
Some practices maybe hold one up a little more clearly.
So I just want to make sure that this distinction is something we're holding very lightly, that the other is always present, in other words.
There's no such thing as stability without insight.
There's no such thing as insight without stability.
Stability is just what it sounds like.
Wouldn't it be great to have a little more stability, to be a little less reactive, to be able, in some literal and figurative way, to more often and more clearly and more fully just feel the ground?
Feel grounded.
And it's funny about a lot of this subtle spiritual stuff is, it's already in the English language.
Grounded.
I want to feel grounded.
Stability is so supported by being quiet, because our complicated voices can be so destabilizing, as important as they are.
It helps stability to be quiet.
It helps stability to slow down a little bit.
And it helps stability to pick a single thing to orient your mind around, and just let that be a marker and a central focus.
Not only does that build the stability of attention, it also helps you see instability, which we don't always see because we're in the middle of it.
It's hard to see what you're in the middle of.
It's like a fish doesn't really see the water.
We don't really see instability and stress because we're so in the middle of it, we're swimming in it.
You ask somebody, "How's your stability today?"
"What?
What are you talking about?"
But it's a thing.
It's actually kind of a thing.
So our central object in Zen is the breath.
The breath in the body.
There's nothing wrong with focusing very strongly on this for years, decades, your whole life, because, like I said, the other piece is included.
A great practice, which I did for many years, is counting the breath.
This sounds like they must have just made that up the other day, like in a psychology lab or something: counting the breath.
It turns out to be thousands of years old.
It's described in very early Chinese Buddhist writings, and I'm sure Indian Buddhist writings before them.
What we recommend, and I'm just going to remind us of some basic things here, so this is old hat to you, just to see it with new eyes.
And if you've never heard of this before, then good, welcome.
You can settle yourself down and arrange your body a little bit in a way that's supportive of stability.
There are various ways to think about the posture, so the spine is in alignment, and there's a certain way of entering the body more fully that's very stabilizing.
So this is not like I'm going to use my mind to find some trick to be more stable.
It's a body and mind activity.
You might take a few deep breaths when you're getting settled, just to open the airways and help you to really, experientially and physically, feel the breathing.
Because we can turn just about anything, well, probably absolutely everything, into an abstraction, into an idea.
What we're interested in is the actual experience of breathing, not the idea of breathing or the rhythm of breathing or something like that.
So a few deep breaths to help us really feel the breathing in the body.
And then finding an area of the body where you can really feel the breathing physically.
The central recommendation in Zen, but I want to put a little caveat on this in a minute, is feeling the breath deep down in the belly.
Of course, anybody who knows any anatomy knows there's no actual air being breathed into the belly.
But through the movement of the diaphragm across the bottom of the ribs, you're feeling the belly, right?
A feeling that results from the process of breathing.
Still, why not imagine the breath coming into the lungs and just filling the belly too?
So, a rising and falling feeling.
But here's the caveat: if that's not accessible to you, feel it somewhere else.
Feel it in the chest, feel it in the throat.
It's much more important to actually feel the breathing than to try to imagine it in the right place because you want to do it right.
Because we're really good at trying to do it right.
And that is not the right way to do things, it turns out.
Once we've found the feeling of the breathing in the body, then just notice the next exhalation and silently mark it as one.
Feel the inhalation come, next exhalation goes, mark it as two.
And three, and so on.
And should you get up to ten, go back to one.
But let those markings, the counting, be so light.
It's not about the counting exactly, but the counting gives our cognitive mind an important role to play.
And do not get caught up in the idea that it's a contest.
Again, not trying to do it right.
The object is not to get to ten.
The instruction is just, if you get to ten, go back to one.
But the minute you hear that, you're like, "Okay, I'm going to see if I can get to ten.
Oh, dang."
This is really hard for most of us.
The process involves going to ten, but it also means going back to one.
Probably a better way to talk about this particular practice, instead of saying breath counting, is to call it "go back to one" counting.
Or "go back to one" breathing.
Because if you lose track of the counting, thinking about something else, or you're not entirely sure, "Am I on four or five?"
That means you're on one.
Back to one.
Back to one.
And one is a beautiful English word.
If English isn't your first language, then use your first language.
One is a beautiful word in all languages.
There's something about unitariness that's really deep.
Just going back to one.
Like I was saying earlier, the great thing about this is it gives you a place to stand in awareness.
And from that place, you can see the rest of your mind a little more clearly.
That's the insight piece.
The counting and awareness of breathing is stabilizing, but the orientation that it supports gives you a little more sense of what's actually going on here.
"I'm worrying about a lot of things.
Oh, look at that, wow.
I'm really distracted by a feeling in my body."
You notice that and you go back to one.
So this is a great practice.
Not to feel like it's the beginner practice and I just need to get good at that, and then maybe the teacher will give me permission to do the cool practice.
You know?
And we think that way too, right?
This is a very deep and important practice, breath counting.
Like all these practices, it's also very portable.
You don't have to be in the Zen meditation hall.
You can practice this while you're walking around, while you're sitting on the bus, while you're taking a minute between things.
Instead of sitting there and instantly half worrying about something that half happened or might happen, which our mind tends to go so quickly to, why don't you just say, "Oh, one, two, three.
What do I have to do next?
Oh, one."

So there's a quality of trust to this too. [unclear: "It's the best in your life to take care of yourself a little more."] A little less need for you to worry about what's happening next, because you don't remember.
Life will remind you.
You'll find out.
So that's a wonderful practice.
If the numbers feel too mechanical or spurious or unnecessary, then do the same thing, but just let go of the counting.
Just feel the breath coming and going.
Feel it as it is and how it is.
In one of the early sutras, early Buddhist teachings,
*the Buddha said the practitioner, when they're having a long breath, [unclear: "they feel.
And no"], I'm having a long breath.
Having a short breath, I know I'm having a short breath.*
So it's not even about having a good kind of breath.
It's just being with the breathing as it is.
This is a central idea here: being with things as they are, with awareness.
You're noticing, you're aware, you're knowing, but letting the knowing be in itself complete.
You can figure out what to do later.
We still have plenty of energy and time for problem solving.
But the mind goes there so often.
So this stability practice is also a deep respite, a refuge, a break from constantly worrying and problem solving.
Or you can open the practice up a little more and hold that breath really lightly.
You might start by establishing awareness of breathing, maybe counting for a little bit.
You can be creative.
Maybe letting the counting go, just breathing.
Maybe letting the breath go.
Let it be so light.
Just a quality of existence.
Being in a body that's breathing, and abandoning the idea that "I'm breathing."
Because that's extra too, right?
The body knows how to breathe.
It doesn't need you mucking with it.
Just let the body breathe you, and be open to whatever's here.
Letting it come, letting it go.
So now we're a little more on the insight side of this equation, stability and insight.
They're always here together.
There's a stability, but as I hold my object of attention more lightly, there's more room for curiosity and movement.
It's not exactly like cataloging or figuring out the mind, but letting the mind be the mind and just knowing it and being in the middle of it, being curious about its patterns and its flow.
The sesshin, the meditation retreat, is such a great place for that, because you see all these patterns in mind that you probably have all the time, but you don't necessarily notice them.
You notice the way they move you and pull you and push you, and the way they can cause tension and suffering or release and joy.
So I was working with a student at this sesshin, somebody I've known for a long time.
I noticed different patterns in my mind as I was trying to be curious about this person and how I could support them in their practice.
At first I felt very spacious and kind and open.
We had an interview meeting, a few suggestions.
It felt very good.
Then we were in a different setting and I had some feedback to give this person, and the person got really reactive.
And I got reactive right back.
It's just like [unclear: "flair"].
I thought I was giving him just a simple little pointer, something that he needs to know, and he was being all reactive and he should know better.
Then I noticed that my perception of this person really changed for the rest of the whole retreat.
I think it was a little sad and disturbing, but it was also interesting.
This is insight, right?
I noticed that person A over here would make a little gesture or do something, and we're supposed to be very silent and composed, and I'd be like, "Oh, okay."
And this person I'm speaking about, he'd make a little gesture and I'd be like, "Stop trying to micromanage the zendo, buddy."
Back to one, back to breathing, back to just being.
So I was in meditation, and Zen doesn't like [unclear: "to hear us from all these foibles"].
But there's much less hold over us when we see them.
We notice them in that particular setting.
I was grateful, even though I was being quite judgmental and reactive, and part of me was quite caught up in this.
There was also a part of me that emerged, that was present, that could say, "Okay, this is reactivity.
This is judgmentalness.
So probably this would not be a good time to give this person good advice."
Just let it be.
Let that subside until I'm in a better place to be helpful in that way.
Right now my helpfulness is restrained.
Another way we can practice, and ideally the best way to determine the way to practice, is to come to us individually.
The best instruction in Zen is individual instruction.
We love for you to come to the interviews, and there's a whole group of us that can give interviews now, so it's always available in all of our practice times.
You don't have to be an established student or have a brilliant question.
You just follow the direction, the invitation.
You got an invitation from Hannah tonight, and you actually believe the invitation, right?
She didn't say, "If you've been here a long time and have a really insightful question, you're invited to put it in your [unclear: "car"]."
She said you're welcome to put it in your [unclear: "car"] and talk to the teacher.
So it's actually true.
Yeah, but we love for you to come and say, "Okay, here's how we've been practicing."
Sometimes just talking to the person, I have some sense of what might be helpful.
Maybe not just from experience or just intuition or something like that.
Maybe the breath counting would be really good to stick to through thick and thin.
Or maybe you know how to let that go, just kind of open to reality.
Or maybe here's another practice we might recommend.
This is a little bit connected to the famous koans of Zen.
Have you heard of the koans of Zen?
They're an often misunderstood part of the Zen tradition, which I won't talk about a lot, but just a little bit tonight.
It's a practice of sitting with a question.
This is another kind of inquiry practice that's also stabilizing.
We think we know what's going on, right?
I'm you and you're me and this is that.
No, it's the other way around.
We get a little mixed up.
But we basically think we know who we are and what's happening and how it all works, and that's a car and that's a dog.
This is my identity, I have this profession and so on and so forth, right?
They always act that way.
All these ideas, how things go.
But from time to time reality reminds us that we're not quite right.
And basically we're a lot not quite right.
Or maybe we're completely not quite right.
So you can practice with the question to increase your natural ability to just be curious, in a really open way.
Curious that doesn't need right away the answer.
We tend to think of questions as always being paired with an answer as fast as possible, right?
That's why we have Google, and we don't have to think anymore.
We can Google.
But this is a pre-Google practice.
So yeah, the teacher might suggest a question to you, and there's a number of simple ones, like "What is it?"
You just sit with that.
Breathing in, breathing out.
What is it?
What is the question in your heart, into the breath, into the ground, into the earth?
Just, what is it?
And just listening.
There may be something that comes back and probably there won't be.
Or maybe a feeling comes back or a sense, or something you can't quite put your finger to comes back.
And this is really supportive of curiosity and openness.
Working with the question or just sitting in an open awareness.
None of it is really that helpful without some degree of stability though.
Just like breath counting that emphasizes stability and return to it regularly.
And all of it is in service not of becoming an excellent meditator.
All of this is in service of living our lives more fully and freely.
And all of this is in service of living our lives more fully and freely so that we can serve.
So that we can be more helpful.
I think when people think about whether to do this practice, right away you think about yourself usually, right?
What am I going to get out of it?
And that's natural, that's where we start.
But then you get into it for a little while and you realize, oh, my presence here is supporting so many other people.
So it's not just about what I get out of it, it's about what I give and it's about what I receive.
And like I said, that's the only reason why you could get up at five in the morning and do silent meditation until nine in the evening.
It's not continuous, there's breaks.
We eat too.
Rest and work and stuff.
It's because it's not just what do I get out of it?
And I think that would never work if the whole idea was just what do I get out of it?
You get so tired and painful very quickly.
And there can be some tiredness and there can be some pain actually.

But as we give ourselves over to a much richer and deeper exchange with stability and curiosity (maybe curiosity is a better word than insight for what I'm trying to get at), insight sounds like something that you get.
This is much more of a process.
And this sort of insight and curiosity starts with the patterns of understanding how our usual self operates.
But then it also opens us up to something bigger than that.
What about what I don't know or can't know or can't put words to?
And every culture throughout history has created some kind of spirituality, right?
Some kind of religion or sense of something beyond this life.
And so they can't all be just making this up out of desperation, right?
There must be a bigger feeling to life, and this practice helps us feel some connection to a bigger feeling of life than just me and what I need and how I get through the day.
When Jeff, my co-teacher Jeff Kelly, and I were giving our talks at the retreat, we were using some simple language, and it seemed helpful there.
Everything is contextual, so I don't know if it was helpful here, but it felt helpful there.
It's the language of limited and unlimited.
So our limited life is like our ordinary life.
It's funny that when I say limited, that sounds like bad.
Like limited is no good.
Oh, that's just really limited.
But is limited bad?
Or is limited just something that has some bounds around it?
It has a sort of circle around it.
Limited is what we can see with our mind, our cognitive mind and our usual way of thinking about things.
And limited is not necessarily bad.
Limited is just limited.
But limited is a wondrous thing too.
It's the world of ideas and relationships and identity and, you know, books and literature and conversations.
It all happens within a limited realm that's bound by language and concepts.
But language and concepts are vast, so the limited world is pretty big.
And yet it is limited.
Somehow words never quite capture the whole thing, right?
The whole feeling for life and for being a person.
That being a person is bigger than any idea of being a person.
And so this kind of curiosity, insight, quality of practice helps us to have more of a feeling or more of a sense for this unlimited quality.
And of course Buddhism's full of language which we've all heard, like enlightenment and awakening, pointing to the same idea.
And there's a million pairings of words, you know, samsara and nirvana for the Buddhist geeks, the born and the unborn, form and emptiness.
We just chanted something about form and emptiness a little while ago.
So limited and unlimited may be another way of speaking about this.
But the unlimited is what's beyond conceptualization.
Inconceivable.
Inconceivable.
Inconceivable is like, wow, right?
Inconceivable.
It sounds really mystical and far out at first, when you hear the word.
Although Jeff started using this word in the talks, and you know what came to me right away?
Have you seen the movie Princess Bride?
The Walshawne character.
The whole movie he runs around, frustrated, because he doesn't like the way things are going, and he keeps saying, "Inconceivable!"
It's just inconceivable that this could be happening.
So I was thinking about Walshawne the whole time.
But anyway, that's the limited side of inconceivable, Walshawne.
He's a wonderful guy, I'm sure of it.
The bigger quality of inconceivable is how our lives are too, right?
We know it's not just this narrative.
There's so much more to my existence, my life, your life.
Or just look at the sky, or really look at a tree.
It's not just some idea of a tree or the sky.
It's vast, it's complex, it's rich, it's subtle.
You can try to describe things.
You can try to describe the sky.
Maybe you read some books about clouds and say, "Oh, there were also cumulus clouds up there."
But that's not the whole thing.

So practice supports us in noticing the inconceivable qualities of our life, and gradually we start to feel and see and remember, on a good day anyway, that there's something bigger going on here than what I can conceptualize and conceive.
And there's a feeling to that which, for some reason I don't really understand, is really freeing, really supportive, really liberating.
We don't have to be caught.
Even though we may have problems, maybe very serious problems, the problem can be met, the problem can be worked with.
We respond to the problem as best we can.
That is the best we can do, right?
The problem held in the spirit of the inconceivable, the unlimited, the open quality of things.
Sometimes we think things as they are, but then the problem is not such a problem.
It's just a problem.
Do you know what I mean?
And in a way everything is inconceivable.
Think about consciousness.
What is it that happens in that moment after something dies?
Or someone dies?
I'm sure at some point in our lives every one of us has been present when a living creature went from alive to not alive.
What happened in that moment?
Something inconceivable changed.
Because it's all the same stuff, right?
The same cells and molecules from point A to point B, just a millisecond apart.
And yet you know, right?
You can see at a glance, even from a distance, if an animal is lying there and it's not alive.
You just know.
So what is that knowing?
Inconceivable.
And sometimes, over the course of a life of practice, we may have some very powerful experiences, really touching or experiencing or interacting with this inconceivable quality in a very direct way.
That can be very powerful, very encouraging.
Also very destabilizing and confusing.
And I think some of us, just by dint of, I don't know what, energetic makeup, are more prone to that kind of experience than others.
I think it would be a big mistake, though, to think that it's about having those kinds of experiences.
Some of us may never have anything that's remotely like that.
For some of us this journey into the inconceivable is much more subtle and quiet.
And gradual.
There's a teaching from Dogen that Suzuki Roshi quotes, that it's like walking through the mist.
The mist is so light you don't even get it that it's misty.
And then you look down and your clothes are damp.
Your robe is wet.
And for some of us, I'm just minding my own business and suddenly I'm in the deep end of the pool.
What's going on?
Whoa!
Far out!
Sometimes people have a big meeting with the inconceivable and then they get really fixated on it for many years.
It becomes this real difficult problem: how do I get that again?
But if we were only in the inconceivable we couldn't function anyway.
It's a recipe for disaster to be too worried about the inconceivable.
And it's a complete recipe for disaster, I think, to not be interested in it at all, to only be lost in the limited life.
So maybe our practice is not about jumping out of this limited world because we don't like limitation.
We're American, right?
Limitation is bad.
But it's about feeling that this limited life is also the unlimited life.
What we can conceive is also inconceivable.
And one of the ways we can explore that is through these practices of meditation: stabilizing, and in that stable space, inviting a lot of curiosity.
What is it?
What is it really?
So anyway, that's my attempt to bring some of what we were talking about at sesshin forward here.
Hope that's helpful.
There are a few ongoing governing bodies in the sangha.
We have a board of directors that oversees the business of the sangha, money and stuff.
And actually, I work for the board.
They could fire me.
So that's one half, the administrative half, which is also spiritual.
Yeah, spiritual and administrative are limited and unlimited too, you know?
So it's very spiritual to go to the administration meeting, when we remember.

We have a practice committee, which advises on matters of practice and schedule, and if I want to make some change to the format of what we do, I run it by those folks and get their input.

I was strongly encouraged.
That was very gentle.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. Good evening. Good to see you. Hannah said something about getting full value from the talk, so I'll try to provide some value. I don't know how to do it though. Because we all have value, and everything we do has value, you know? So I think it is so easy for us to sort of imagine in our minds that one part of something is the important part, and the other part is the warm up, and the other part is the after work, or something like that.

So I just came back from a five day retreat, five day sesshin, we call them Zen meditation retreat. And at one point I was given one of the talks, and it occurred to me, I wonder if it's really like the talk that's important, or the bowing before the talk, or the meditation, like who knows what's really important. or whatever parts of our body that were feeling a little bit difficult. It's such a powerful practice, you know, the practice we call sesshin. And so it's not so much like figuring anything out, or calming down, or getting better at something, but it's like what about if we really had some time to just really touch in, you know, what's here, can I kind of make contact, make contact with myself in some way.
